title: Newton's laws: draw the forces before the equation

chapters.title: Choose the body and draw its forces
points: Choose one body and an approximately inertial frame.
Draw only external forces acting on that body.
Constant velocity does not require a nonzero net force.
chapters.script: Welcome back. In straight line motion, we described how velocity changes. Today we ask why it changes. Imagine pushing a box across a floor. Before writing an equation, choose the box as the body you are studying. Draw its weight downward, the floor's normal reaction upward, your push to the right, and friction to the left if the box tends to slide right. This is a free body diagram. Every arrow must name a real interaction. Do not draw an extra arrow called motion or acceleration. Acceleration is the result we calculate. Now imagine the forces balance. Must the box be stationary? Take a moment to think. No. Newton's first law says zero net force means constant velocity in an inertial frame. That constant velocity may be zero, but it does not have to be. For ordinary classroom problems we usually treat the ground as approximately inertial. A useful way to test your diagram is to ask who is exerting each force. Earth supplies weight. The floor supplies contact forces. Your hand supplies the push. In JEE problems, getting this picture right often matters more than the algebra that follows.

chapters.title: Add the forces before dividing by mass
chapters.formula: Sum of F(x) = m a(x); Sum of F(y) = m a(y)
points: Choose positive directions before assigning signs.
14 N right minus 4 N left gives 10 N right.
chapters.script: Newton's second law connects the diagram to motion. For a constant mass, the vector sum of external forces equals mass times acceleration. Notice the word sum. One force alone does not tell you the acceleration when several forces act. Choose right as positive. A five kilogram box has a fourteen newton pull to the right and four newtons of friction to the left. Before calculating, predict the direction. The rightward force wins. The net force is fourteen minus four, or ten newtons to the right. Divide by five kilograms to get two metres per second squared. We subtract because the forces oppose each other. Now separate the vertical direction. If the box has no vertical acceleration, and only weight and the normal reaction act vertically, the normal reaction equals its weight. That conclusion follows from the vertical equation. It is not a universal rule. An upward angled pull would reduce the floor's required reaction. A lift accelerating upward would change it too. Here is your exam routine: draw the body, choose axes, resolve forces, add signed components, then divide by mass. Check that the acceleration points in the direction of the net force, even when the body is currently moving the other way.

chapters.title: Third-law pairs belong to different bodies
chapters.formula: Force of A on B = minus force of B on A
points: A third-law pair describes one interaction between two bodies.
The two forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction.
Weight and normal reaction on the same book are not a third-law pair.
chapters.script: If every force has an equal and opposite partner, why does anything accelerate? The answer is in the body you selected. When your hand pushes a box, the box pushes your hand with equal magnitude and opposite direction. The force on the box belongs on the box's diagram. The force on your hand belongs on your hand's diagram. They do not cancel in the net force on the box alone. Try a common JEE trap. A book rests on a table. Its weight points downward and the normal reaction points upward. Are these a third law pair? Think about which bodies receive the forces. Both forces act on the book, so they are not partners under the third law. The partner of Earth's gravitational pull on the book is the book's gravitational pull on Earth. The partner of the table's contact force on the book is the book's contact force on the table. Equal magnitudes do not by themselves identify a pair. Name the interaction and reverse the giver and receiver. That is the reliable test. The two forces act simultaneously; the words action and reaction do not mean that one force happens later.

chapters.title: Static friction adjusts; sliding friction changes the calculation
chapters.formula: Static: |f| <= mu(s) N; Sliding: |f| = mu(k) N
points: 4 kg and g = 10 m/s² give N = 40 N on a horizontal floor.
mu(s) = 0.5 gives a maximum static friction of 20 N.
12 N push: rest; 28 N push: sliding, with acceleration 4 m/s².
chapters.script: Friction is where a correct formula can still give a wrong answer if you choose the wrong situation. Static friction adjusts to prevent relative slipping, up to a limit. It does not always equal that limit. Consider a four kilogram block initially at rest on a horizontal floor. Use g equal to ten metres per second squared, as specified in this example. The normal reaction is forty newtons. Let the static friction coefficient be zero point five and the kinetic coefficient zero point three. The maximum static friction is twenty newtons. Now push with twelve newtons. Will it move? Pause and compare twelve with the limit. Static friction can supply twelve newtons in the opposite direction, so the block stays at rest. Its actual friction is twelve, not twenty. Next increase the push to twenty eight newtons. Rest is no longer possible because the required friction exceeds twenty. Once the block slides, use kinetic friction: zero point three times forty equals twelve newtons. The net force is twenty eight minus twelve, or sixteen newtons. Divide by four kilograms and the acceleration is four metres per second squared. Friction opposes relative slipping at the contact, or its tendency. It does not always oppose the body's overall motion: static friction can push a walking person forward. Always identify the contact and its slipping tendency first.

chapters.title: Rotate your axes for an incline
chapters.formula: N = mg cos(theta); frictionless a = g sin(theta)
points: Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
Weight has components mg sin(theta) down and mg cos(theta) into the slope.
At 30 degrees with g = 10: a = 5 m/s²; for 2 kg, N = 10 sqrt(3) N.
chapters.script: On a slope, a better choice of axes makes the problem simpler. Choose one axis down the slope and another perpendicular to it. Weight still points vertically downward. Its component down the slope is m g sine theta, and its component into the slope is m g cosine theta, where theta is the incline's angle to the horizontal. The normal reaction balances the perpendicular component if no other perpendicular forces act and there is no perpendicular acceleration. It therefore equals m g cosine theta. Let us solve a two kilogram block sliding on a frictionless thirty degree incline, using g equal to ten. First predict whether the acceleration depends on mass. The downslope force is two times ten times one half, or ten newtons. Divide by two kilograms to get five metres per second squared down the slope. Mass cancels. The normal reaction is twenty times cosine thirty degrees, which is ten times the square root of three newtons, about seventeen point three. It is perpendicular to the slope, not vertical. If the block slides downward with kinetic friction, subtract mu k times the normal reaction from the downslope force before dividing by mass. An upslope acceleration can slow a block that is still moving downward. Finish every force problem with four checks: one body, clear axes, correct contact model, and consistent units. Complete the practice questions next, and keep the written lesson open for the worked solutions.
